title: Blood Supply of the Endocrine Glands
subject: Endocrine System (ENDO)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: Endocrine glands secrete into blood, so the way blood enters and leaves each gland shapes how its hormones work and how the gland fails. This chapter traces the vessels of the thyroid, pituitary, adrenals, parathyroids, and pancreatic islets, then uses that anatomy to explain four classic exam problems: why the anterior pituitary infarcts after postpartum hemorrhage, why the adrenal medulla makes mostly epinephrine, why calcium falls after thyroid surgery, and why the liver sees insulin before any other tissue. Board questions usually give the clinical event and ask you to name the vessel, the hormone that changed, or the lab pattern that follows.
prerequisites: Branches of the external carotid, subclavian, and abdominal aorta
Embryology of the pituitary (Rathke pouch and neurohypophysis) and pharyngeal pouches
Hypothalamic releasing hormones and anterior pituitary axes (EN-3)
PTH and vitamin D control of plasma calcium
Insulin synthesis from proinsulin and hepatic glucose metabolism

connections.how: The portal system is the delivery route that makes hypothalamic control of the anterior pituitary possible.
Loss of parathyroid blood supply removes PTH and produces the predictable lab pattern of low calcium with high phosphate.
Cortisol carried from cortex to medulla induces PNMT, the final enzyme of epinephrine synthesis.
Pancreatic venous drainage into the portal vein sets up hepatic first-pass extraction of insulin.
The thyroid arteries run with the external laryngeal and recurrent laryngeal nerves, linking vascular anatomy to voice changes.

terms.def: A circulation in which blood passes through two capillary beds in series, connected by veins, before returning to the heart.
The base of the hypothalamus where hypothalamic axons end on fenestrated capillaries outside the blood-brain barrier.
A capillary whose endothelium has pores that let hormones and other solutes pass freely between cells and blood.
An artery that is the only blood supply to its territory, with too few anastomoses to rescue the tissue if it is blocked.
An inconstant midline artery, present in about 10% of people, that ascends in front of the trachea to the thyroid isthmus.
Ischemic necrosis of the anterior pituitary after severe postpartum hemorrhage, causing hypopituitarism.
A neural crest derived cell of the adrenal medulla that synthesizes and secretes catecholamines.
Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase, the cytosolic enzyme that methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine using S-adenosylmethionine.
Removal of a substance by the liver during its first passage through the portal circulation, before it reaches the systemic blood.
The connecting peptide cut from proinsulin and secreted in equimolar amounts with insulin, with little hepatic clearance.
Involuntary muscle spasm caused by increased nerve excitability, classically from low ionized calcium.

sections.title: Arteries and veins of the thyroid gland

blocks.text: The thyroid has one of the highest blood flows per gram of any organ. Each follicle is wrapped in fenestrated capillaries that deliver iodide for hormone synthesis and carry thyroxine (T4) and triiodothyronine (T3) away. Two arteries reach each lobe, and they anastomose freely with each other and across the midline, so tying a single artery rarely leaves the gland ischemic.

The superior thyroid artery is usually the first anterior branch of the external carotid artery. It descends to the upper pole of the lobe alongside the external branch of the superior laryngeal nerve, which supplies the cricothyroid muscle. The inferior thyroid artery comes from the thyrocervical trunk, a branch of the first part of the subclavian artery. It ascends, then turns medially behind the carotid sheath to enter the lower posterior surface of the lobe, where its branches cross the recurrent laryngeal nerve in the tracheoesophageal groove. In about 10% of people a thyroid ima artery, most often from the brachiocephalic trunk, ascends in front of the trachea to the isthmus.

blocks.title: Vessels of the thyroid
rows: External branch of the superior laryngeal nerve
Thyrocervical trunk of the subclavian artery
Recurrent laryngeal nerve; main supply of the parathyroids
Usually brachiocephalic trunk; sometimes aortic arch or other neck arteries
Lies in front of the trachea below the isthmus
Travels with the superior thyroid artery
Short vein with no accompanying artery
Form a plexus in front of the trachea; no accompanying artery
blocks.caption: Arteries and veins do not mirror each other: the inferior thyroid artery comes from the subclavian system, but the inferior veins drain to the brachiocephalic veins.

blocks.text: Several findings follow directly from this anatomy. In Graves disease, antibodies that stimulate the TSH receptor cause follicular hyperplasia and greatly increased vascularity, which can produce a palpable thrill and an audible bruit over the gland. The inferior thyroid veins and, when present, the thyroid ima artery lie in front of the trachea below the isthmus, so they are the vessels at risk in a low midline tracheostomy. Because each artery travels with a nerve, injury near the superior thyroid artery can paralyze the cricothyroid and cause a weak voice that cannot reach high pitch, and injury near the inferior thyroid artery can damage the recurrent laryngeal nerve and cause hoarseness.

sections.title: The hypothalamo-hypophyseal portal system and anterior pituitary ischemia

blocks.text: The two pituitary lobes have different origins and different blood supplies. The posterior lobe (neurohypophysis) grows down from the diencephalon and contains the axon terminals of hypothalamic neurons, which release antidiuretic hormone and oxytocin into capillaries fed directly by the inferior hypophyseal arteries from the cavernous part of the internal carotid artery. The anterior lobe (adenohypophysis) comes from Rathke pouch, has no neural connection to the hypothalamus, and is controlled entirely through blood.

The superior hypophyseal arteries leave the internal carotid artery just above the cavernous sinus and form a primary capillary plexus in the median eminence and upper stalk. These capillaries are fenestrated and lie outside the blood-brain barrier, so peptides and dopamine released by hypothalamic neurons enter them freely. Long portal veins carry this blood down the stalk to a second bed of sinusoids among the anterior lobe cells, and short portal veins bring additional portal blood from the lower stalk. Anterior pituitary hormones enter the same sinusoids and leave through the cavernous sinuses and petrosal sinuses.

blocks.title: Hypophyseal portal transport
steps: Superior hypophyseal arteries supply the median eminence
Hypothalamic neurons release releasing hormones and dopamine there
Hormones enter the fenestrated primary capillary plexus
Portal veins carry them down the pituitary stalk
Secondary sinusoids deliver them to anterior pituitary cells
Pituitary hormones drain to the cavernous sinuses
blocks.caption: Two capillary beds in series let small amounts of hypothalamic hormone reach the anterior lobe undiluted by the systemic circulation.

blocks.text: The portal route matters because releasing hormones are secreted in tiny amounts and last only minutes. Diluted in the whole blood volume they would be ineffective, but in portal blood they arrive concentrated and their pulsatile pattern is preserved. Dopamine reaching lactotrophs by this route tonically inhibits prolactin release, so cutting or compressing the stalk lowers every anterior pituitary hormone except prolactin, which rises.

The same arrangement makes the anterior lobe vulnerable. Nearly all of its blood arrives through portal veins after passing through one capillary bed already, so its perfusion pressure is low and it has almost no direct arterial supply to fall back on. In pregnancy, estrogen-driven lactotroph hyperplasia enlarges the gland inside the rigid sella turcica, raising its demand for blood. If severe postpartum hemorrhage causes hypotension (vasospasm of the supplying arteries may contribute), the anterior lobe can infarct (Sheehan syndrome). The posterior lobe, with its own arterial supply, is usually spared. Clinical hypopituitarism appears once most of the anterior lobe is destroyed.

blocks.title: Hormone losses in Sheehan syndrome
rows: Failure to lactate, often the first sign
No stimulus to milk production after delivery
Low T4 with low or inappropriately normal TSH
Secondary adrenal insufficiency: fatigue, hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia
Low cortisol; aldosterone preserved by renin-angiotensin, so no hyperkalemia; low POMC, so no hyperpigmentation
Loss of GH counterregulation and anabolic effects
blocks.caption: Every anterior lobe axis can fail; ADH and oxytocin are usually preserved because the posterior lobe has a separate arterial supply.

blocks.predict: A tumor compresses the pituitary stalk without touching the gland. Which anterior pituitary hormone rises?
blocks.explain: Prolactin. Compression interrupts portal delivery of dopamine, removing the tonic inhibition of lactotrophs, while the other axes lose their releasing hormones and fall.
blocks.check: The paragraph on why the portal route matters.

sections.title: Adrenal vessels and the cortex-to-medulla route that induces PNMT

blocks.text: Each adrenal gland receives three sets of arteries, which break into many small branches forming a plexus under the capsule, but drains through a single vein.

blocks.title: Adrenal vessels
rows: Directly into the inferior vena cava (short vein)
Left renal vein, often joined by the left inferior phrenic vein
blocks.caption: Three arterial sources and one vein per side; like the left gonadal vein, the left suprarenal vein ends in the left renal vein, while the right drains straight into the IVC.

blocks.text: Inside the gland, blood follows three routes. Capsular vessels supply the capsule. Most blood enters fenestrated cortical sinusoids and flows centripetally through the zona glomerulosa, fasciculata, and reticularis into the medullary capillaries, collecting cortisol on the way. A smaller set of medullary arteries passes straight through the cortex, giving the medulla fresh arterial blood as well. All routes empty into a central medullary vein whose wall contains bundles of longitudinal smooth muscle.

The venous asymmetry has practical meaning. In adrenal vein sampling, used to decide whether excess aldosterone comes from one gland or both, the short right vein entering the back of the inferior vena cava is much harder to catheterize than the left vein, which is reached through the left renal vein.

Chromaffin cells make catecholamines from tyrosine. Tyrosine hydroxylase (the rate-limiting step) forms DOPA, which becomes dopamine; dopamine enters secretory granules and is converted to norepinephrine by dopamine beta-hydroxylase. Norepinephrine then leaks into the cytosol, where PNMT transfers a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine to form epinephrine, which is pumped back into granules. PNMT expression depends on high glucocorticoid levels. Because sinusoidal blood reaching the medulla has just passed through the cortex, its cortisol concentration is many times the systemic level, and this local cortisol keeps PNMT induced. As a result, about 80% of adult adrenal medullary output is epinephrine.

blocks.title: From cortical cortisol to medullary epinephrine
steps: Suprarenal arteries feed the subcapsular plexus
Blood flows inward through cortical sinusoids
Zona fasciculata adds cortisol at very high concentration
Cortisol-rich blood bathes medullary chromaffin cells
Cortisol induces PNMT in the cytosol
PNMT methylates norepinephrine to epinephrine
Central vein drains to IVC or left renal vein
blocks.caption: The intra-adrenal portal-like flow from cortex to medulla links glucocorticoid output to epinephrine synthesis.

blocks.text: Several distinctions follow. Chromaffin tissue outside the adrenal (paraganglia, including the organ of Zuckerkandl near the aortic bifurcation) does not receive cortisol-rich blood, so it secretes mainly norepinephrine, and extra-adrenal paragangliomas are usually norepinephrine-predominant. A tumor secreting large amounts of epinephrine points to an adrenal origin. When cortisol production falls, as in ACTH deficiency or destruction of the cortex, PNMT activity and epinephrine output can fall as well.

blocks.predict: A catecholamine-secreting tumor sits beside the aortic bifurcation. Would you expect it to secrete mainly epinephrine or norepinephrine?
blocks.explain: Mainly norepinephrine. Outside the adrenal, chromaffin cells do not receive blood that has passed through the cortex, so cortisol is too low to sustain PNMT expression.
blocks.check: The flow figure and the paragraph on extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue.

sections.title: Parathyroid blood supply and hypocalcemia after thyroidectomy

blocks.text: There are usually four parathyroid glands, each weighing only a few tens of milligrams, on the posterior surface of the thyroid lobes. The superior pair develops from the fourth pharyngeal pouch and stays in a fairly constant position near the cricothyroid junction. The inferior pair develops from the third pouch, descends with the thymus, and varies more in position, sometimes lying low in the neck or in the mediastinum.

Each gland is supplied by a single tiny parathyroid artery that enters at its hilum and behaves as an end artery. For the inferior glands, and for most superior glands, this artery is a branch of the inferior thyroid artery, because that artery divides on the posterior surface of the lobe exactly where the glands lie; in some people the superior glands are supplied by the superior thyroid artery or by an anastomosis between the two. Venous blood drains into the thyroid venous plexus. Because the glands are small, tan, and easily mistaken for fat or lymph nodes, and because their arteries run on the gland surface where dissection occurs, thyroid surgery can remove them or cut off their blood supply. A devascularized gland stops secreting just as a removed gland does.
PTH has a plasma half-life of only a few minutes, so when secretion stops, PTH falls within hours. Plasma calcium then falls over the next 1 to 3 days as each PTH action is lost.

blocks.title: Hypocalcemia after loss of parathyroid supply
steps: Parathyroid arteries are divided, or glands removed
PTH secretion stops; PTH falls within hours
Osteoclastic bone resorption decreases
Distal tubule calcium reabsorption decreases
Renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase falls, so calcitriol falls
Intestinal calcium absorption decreases
Ionized calcium falls; phosphate rises from reduced phosphaturia
blocks.caption: Bone, kidney, and gut all deliver less calcium to plasma once PTH is gone.

blocks.text: Normal total calcium is about 8.5 to 10.5 mg/dL (2.1 to 2.6 mmol/L), and ionized calcium about 4.5 to 5.3 mg/dL (1.1 to 1.3 mmol/L). Low extracellular calcium lets voltage-gated Na+ channels open at less depolarized potentials, lowering the firing threshold of nerves. Peripheral nerves then fire spontaneously, giving perioral and fingertip tingling, muscle cramps, carpopedal spasm, and in severe cases laryngospasm or seizures. Tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear causes twitching of the facial muscles (Chvostek sign), and inflating a blood pressure cuff above systolic pressure for about 3 minutes causes carpal spasm (Trousseau sign). On the ECG the ST segment lengthens, prolonging the QT interval.

Two other causes of low calcium after neck surgery must be separated. In hungry bone syndrome, after surgery for long-standing hyperparathyroidism or hyperthyroidism, demineralized bone rapidly takes up calcium and phosphate, so calcium and phosphate are both low while PTH is normal or high. Hyperventilation from pain or anxiety causes respiratory alkalosis, which increases calcium binding to albumin and lowers ionized calcium without changing total calcium.

blocks.title: Interpreting calcium 36 hours after thyroidectomy
blocks.text: A patient reports perioral tingling 36 hours after total thyroidectomy. Total calcium is 7.0 mg/dL, albumin 3.0 g/dL, phosphate 5.8 mg/dL (normal about 2.5 to 4.5), and PTH is undetectable. Step 1: correct for albumin. Each 1 g/dL of albumin below 4.0 lowers total calcium by about 0.8 mg/dL, so corrected calcium is 7.0 + 0.8 = 7.8 mg/dL, still low. Step 2: read phosphate. It is high, which means PTH is not driving phosphaturia. Step 3: read PTH. It is inappropriately low for the hypocalcemia. Low calcium, high phosphate, and low PTH together indicate hypoparathyroidism from devascularized or removed glands, not hungry bone syndrome, where phosphate would be low and PTH normal or high.

sections.title: Portal drainage of islet hormones and hepatic first-pass extraction of insulin

blocks.text: Islets make up only about 1 to 2% of pancreatic mass but receive a much larger share of pancreatic blood flow. Their arteries come from pancreatic branches of the splenic artery and from the superior and inferior pancreaticoduodenal arteries (branches of the gastroduodenal and superior mesenteric arteries). Within each islet an afferent arteriole breaks into a dense network of fenestrated capillaries, so hormone enters blood almost as soon as it is secreted. Some efferent blood passes on to surrounding acinar capillaries, but all of it eventually leaves through pancreatic veins that join the splenic vein (body and tail) and the superior mesenteric vein (head). These two veins unite behind the neck of the pancreas to form the hepatic portal vein.

blocks.title: Route of secreted insulin
steps: Beta cells secrete insulin and C-peptide into islet capillaries
Pancreatic veins drain to splenic and superior mesenteric veins
Hepatic portal vein carries hormones to the liver
Hepatocytes bind and degrade about half the insulin
Hepatic veins carry the remainder into the systemic circulation
Muscle and fat receive lower insulin; kidneys clear much of it
blocks.caption: The liver is both the first target and the first clearance site for secreted insulin; C-peptide passes through largely untouched.

blocks.text: This anatomy places the liver, the main organ buffering blood glucose, first in line. Portal insulin concentration is normally about two to three times the peripheral level, and portal glucagon is also higher than peripheral. The liver responds to the portal insulin-to-glucagon ratio: insulin suppresses glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis and promotes glycogen storage, while glucagon acts through cAMP to do the opposite. Glucagon acts mainly on the liver, because skeletal muscle has essentially no glucagon receptors, so portal drainage delivers it straight to its main target.

Hepatocytes take up insulin by receptor-mediated endocytosis and degrade it, largely through insulin-degrading enzyme. About half of the insulin in portal blood is removed on the first pass, though the fraction varies with physiological state. The kidneys clear much of the insulin that reaches the systemic circulation, and plasma insulin has a half-life of about 5 minutes. C-peptide is cut from proinsulin inside the same secretory granules and released in equimolar amounts, but the liver extracts very little of it. It is cleared mainly by the kidney and has a half-life of about 30 minutes, so peripheral C-peptide exceeds insulin on a molar basis and tracks secretion more faithfully.

blocks.title: Reading insulin and C-peptide
rows: Hepatic first-pass extraction of insulin but not C-peptide
Beta cells are secreting proinsulin-derived insulin
Exogenous insulin contains no C-peptide and suppresses beta cells
Less hepatic extraction lets more insulin reach the periphery
blocks.caption: Insulin reflects secretion minus hepatic and renal clearance; C-peptide reflects secretion.

blocks.text: Injected insulin reverses the normal gradient: it enters the systemic circulation first, so muscle and fat receive relatively more and the liver relatively less than with secreted insulin. Renal failure slows systemic insulin clearance and so prolongs insulin action.

blocks.title: Using C-peptide to locate the source of insulin
blocks.text: Two adults have fasting hypoglycemia with glucose about 40 mg/dL (2.2 mmol/L). In both, insulin is high, which is inappropriate because hypoglycemia should switch secretion off. Patient A has high C-peptide and proinsulin. Because C-peptide is released only when beta cells cleave proinsulin, the excess insulin is being secreted, as with an insulinoma or a sulfonylurea effect. Patient B has suppressed C-peptide. The high insulin cannot come from beta cells, so it must be exogenous. The portal anatomy explains why C-peptide is the better marker: insulin is variably extracted by the liver before it is measured, but C-peptide is not.

integration.text: Anatomy and embryology explain the supply: the anterior pituitary, derived from oral ectoderm with no neural link to the hypothalamus, depends on portal blood; the parathyroids, from the pharyngeal pouches, sit on the thyroid and borrow its inferior artery; and the pancreas drains to the portal vein because it develops from foregut endoderm within the territory of the gut circulation. Physiology and biochemistry explain why the arrangement is useful, because portal and portal-like routes deliver hormones at high concentration to the cells that need them most: releasing hormones to the anterior lobe, cortisol to the medulla, and insulin and glucagon to the liver.

Pathology shows the cost of the same designs. Low-pressure portal supply makes the enlarged anterior pituitary infarct when blood pressure falls, end arteries make the parathyroids easy to devascularize, and portal drainage makes peripheral insulin an imperfect measure of secretion. The limits matter as well: arterial patterns vary between people, the posterior pituitary is spared only because it has a separate supply, and lab values must be read together, since calcium, phosphate, PTH, insulin, and C-peptide each change for more than one reason.

summary: The superior thyroid artery comes from the external carotid and the inferior thyroid artery from the thyrocervical trunk; a thyroid ima artery is present in about 10% of people.
Superior and middle thyroid veins drain to the internal jugular; inferior thyroid veins drain to the brachiocephalic veins in front of the trachea.
Superior hypophyseal arteries feed the median eminence plexus, and portal veins carry releasing hormones and dopamine to the anterior lobe's sinusoids.

The anterior pituitary depends on low-pressure portal blood, so the pregnancy-enlarged lobe infarcts with postpartum hypotension (Sheehan syndrome), while the arterially supplied posterior lobe is spared.
Stalk compression lowers every anterior pituitary hormone except prolactin, which rises when portal dopamine is lost.
Each adrenal has superior (inferior phrenic), middle (aorta), and inferior (renal) arteries and one vein: right to the IVC, left to the left renal vein.
Blood flows from cortex to medulla, and the high local cortisol induces PNMT, so the medulla secretes mainly epinephrine while extra-adrenal chromaffin tissue secretes norepinephrine.
The parathyroids depend on small end arteries, mainly from the inferior thyroid artery, so thyroidectomy can cause hypocalcemia with high phosphate and low PTH within 1 to 3 days.
Islet hormones drain into the portal vein, so the liver sees insulin and glucagon first and removes about half the insulin on first pass.
C-peptide escapes hepatic extraction and reflects beta-cell secretion: high in insulinoma, low after injected insulin.

verify: The prevalence of a thyroid ima artery is quoted as about 3% to 10% in different anatomical series; this chapter uses about 10% (Moore).
The fraction of anterior pituitary blood that arrives through portal vessels is quoted variably (often 70% to 90% or more); the chapter says nearly all without a number.
The extent of anterior pituitary destruction before hypopituitarism is clinically evident is often given as about 75%; confirm the figure NABNE expects if it is tested.
The intra-adrenal cortisol concentration reaching the medulla is described only as many times the systemic level because published ratios vary widely.
The proportion of adrenal medullary output that is epinephrine (about 80%) follows Guyton and Hall; other sources give 75% to 85%.
Hepatic first-pass extraction of insulin is quoted from about 40% to 80%, and the portal to peripheral insulin ratio from about 2 to 3 or higher; values here are stated as approximate.
The share of pancreatic blood flow reaching the islets is often cited as about 5% to 10% despite 1% to 2% of mass; the chapter avoids a single figure.
Ionized calcium reference ranges vary slightly by laboratory; the albumin correction of 0.8 mg/dL per 1 g/dL is a convention of limited accuracy.
Confirm whether NABNE Part I expects the eponyms organ of Zuckerkandl, Chvostek sign, and Trousseau sign, or only the descriptive findings.
